_purpose: Ground-truth facts about @sanity/vision's package format, extracted directly from the installed package's package.json (not inferred). This is why require() crashes and why an ESM import is the only mechanically valid fix. If @sanity/vision is ever bumped, re-extract this file before trusting it -- VF-07 in the contract cross-checks the live node_modules/@sanity/vision/package.json against the 'type' field and will fail loudly if it drifts.

@sanity/vision.why_require_crashes: "type": "module" means every .js file in this package (including the ./lib/index.js pointed to by "main") is parsed as an ES module by Node and by bundlers that respect package.json's module-type field. There is no separate CJS build and no "require" condition in the "exports" map. A CommonJS require('@sanity/vision') has no valid entry point to resolve to -- this is a hard incompatibility, not a bundler misconfiguration. Next.js's webpack detects this and refuses to proceed, producing the confirmed 'Module not found: ESM packages (@sanity/vision) need to be imported' error and a 500 on the /studio route.
@sanity/vision.why_sideEffects_matters_for_the_fix_choi: sideEffects is scoped to only ["*.css", "*.css.ts"] -- meaning every plain .js/.ts module in this package (including lib/index.js, which exports visionTool) is explicitly marked side-effect-free. This is what allows webpack's tree-shaking / unused-export elimination to safely drop an unused static import of visionTool from the production bundle when the reference to it is inside a branch that's statically known to be false at build time (see README.md's 'Fix pattern decision' section for the full reasoning chain). Without this field (or with it defaulting to true), a static top-level import would be a bundle-size regression risk; with it, it is not.

authoring_time_build_baseline.note: Captured against the CURRENT (unfixed, buggy) sanity.config.ts to establish a pre-fix baseline for VF-05 -- confirms the crash is dev-only, not a general build failure.
authoring_time_build_baseline.pnpm_build_result: SUCCEEDS today even with the unfixed require() present
authoring_time_build_baseline.why_build_does_not_crash: Next.js's webpack replaces process.env.NODE_ENV with the literal "production" during a production build (DefinePlugin), and webpack's parser (ConstPlugin) recognizes `if (process.env.NODE_ENV === 'development')` as a statically-false branch and skips adding its require()/import() dependency to the module graph entirely -- before dependency resolution, not just as a post-hoc dead-code-elimination pass. The require() is never actually reached or resolved during `pnpm build`. Under `pnpm dev`, NODE_ENV genuinely is 'development', the branch IS reached, and the require() must actually resolve -- that is where and why it crashes.
